input.question: Why didn't we actively re-center the ranges to follow the price (frequent narrowing), instead of staying wide?
input.reference: On 720 days 0 of 21 narrow configurations passed the gate, and the one live narrowing (31.08 to 11.09) ended -$32 vs HODL, so on 16.09 narrowing was rejected again because the upside (about +$1 per episode) is far smaller than the loss when the price leaves a ±5% range (about -$30).
input.answer: The project rejected frequent narrowing because backtests showed the extra fees earned did not compensate for the costs. Narrow ranges generated 4x more fees, but the implied loss (IL) from re-centering wiped out that advantage, leaving net returns lower than a passive wide range. This was true even in flat market conditions, where narrowing theoretically should have an edge. The analysis concluded that the wide passive strategy was superior.

narrowing added variance without adding expectancy at the flat-episode lengths actually observed (median 7.7 days).

input.question: Why did the LP earn less in fees during an uptrend than in a flat market?
input.reference: Fees accrue only while the price is inside the range and fee yield scales roughly with 1/width, so a narrow range earns much more in a flat market but is left behind in a trend, while a wide range stays in range but earns several times less; the journal states this mechanism (the basis of FlatWide) but has no live measurement of fees during an uptrend, and it attributes the backtest losses in up windows to impermanent loss and LVR rather than to lower fees.
input.answer: The LP earned less in fees during an uptrend because concentrated liquidity forces the provider to sell into rallies and buy into drawdowns. This convexity cost outweighs the fee income in trending markets. Specifically, when the price moves out of the concentrated range, the position becomes 100% in one token, meaning it pays no further fees while also realizing impermanent loss.

quotes.quote: you sell into rallies and buy into drawdowns, and in a trending year that costs more than fees earn
a position 100% in one token pays no fees

verdict.correctnessReason: The answer captures that an out-of-range position earns no fees, but it conflates convexity/IL losses with lower fee income and misses the range-width tradeoff and the journal's lack of any live uptrend fee measurement.
verdict.faithfulnessReason: The quotes back the sell-into-rallies cost and the no-fees-when-100%-one-token claim, but not the realized impermanent loss claim or the framing that this explains lower fees.

input.question: Is FLAT_NARROW a specific position or some kind of range algorithm?
input.reference: Neither: it is a proposal type (kind) emitted by the bot's flat detector when the flat regime is confirmed (|gap to the EMA| < 2% for at least 12 h), proposing to narrow an existing wide position to a fixed ±5%, with FLAT_WIDEN as the opposite card when |gap| > 5%; unsigned cards expire on a TTL and come back.
input.answer: FLAT_NARROW is a specific proposal kind (an action), not a standalone range algorithm. It is part of the "FlatWide" product and triggers when a pool's flat state is confirmed (|gap|<2% for ≥12h). The action narrows the existing position's range from a wider band (e.g., ±40% or ±50%) down to a fixed product width of ±5% (1.0× exit threshold) to capture higher fees during the flat episode. It is paired with FLAT_WIDEN, which reverts the range to a wider ±productIdleWidthPct once the flat ends. The proposal includes specific `suggestedRange` tick bounds, cost, and payback days for that specific pool position.

input.question: What does the function fetchFreshPool do?
input.reference: It re-reads the pool state on-chain (factory.getPool, then slot0 and liquidity) right before the mint step of a rebalance or rotation, so the new position is built from the current price instead of the price captured when the modal opened, and falls back to the old pool if the lookup fails; it was added after the 11.09 widening failed once on 'Price slippage check' and was never exercised live, since the only later chance (a FLAT_NARROW card on 16.09) was not signed and the positions were closed by hand in Uniswap.
input.answer: fetchFreshPool refreshes the on-chain pool state before executing a rebalance or rotation. It calls factory.getPool to get the pool address, reads slot0 (current tick/price) and liquidity from that address, and constructs a new Pool object with the same tokens and fee tier. It is fail-open: if the factory or RPC call fails, it returns the previous pool object instead of throwing. It is wired into useRebalanceExecution and useRotateExecution immediately before buildMintStep. A noted caveat is that the range tick bounds still come from the original plan (computed at the old price), so after a price move the range is slightly off-center.

wpięty w `useRebalanceExecution` i `useRotateExecution` tuż przed `buildMintStep`
ticki zakresu nadal z planu (liczone przy starym kursie), więc po ruchu ceny zakres jest lekko niecentryczny
